description:
FILED s470bs (Opus) from #1042's own instruction to "sweep that whole family":
anything initialised from a defvar INITFORM that must be per-RUN rather than
per-IMAGE.  This one is not a saved-core problem â it is wrong in a fresh
process too â but it came out of the same audit and belongs beside it.

    (defvar *p-drand48-state* (logior (ash 0 16) #x330e) â¦)

The seed is the literal 0.  `p-srand` sets it properly when a program calls
`srand`, and `p-rand` never seeds; so

    perl -e 'print rand, "\n"'   twice   ->  two different numbers
    ./runpcl  the same program   twice   ->  the SAME number

perl seeds PL_random from entropy at first use of `rand` (and `srand` without
an argument returns the seed it chose).  PCL's `p-srand` with no argument uses
`(get-universal-time)`, so the SEEDING code is there; nothing calls it.

WHAT THE AUDIT FOUND, for the record (s470bs, the #1042 family):
  * `$^T`   â WAS frozen into the saved core.  FIXED in s470bs by an
              `sb-ext:*init-hooks*` entry, the pattern `$$` already used.
  * `$$`    â already has that hook (added with the core work).
  * `$0`    â its initform reads `(car sb-ext:*posix-argv*)` at LOAD, so a
              saved core carries the BUILD argv[0].  Measured harmless: SBCL
              is argv[0] either way, and pl2cl's preamble overwrites `$0` with
              the script name at program load.  LEFT ALONE deliberately.
  * `%ENV`  â a marker resolved dynamically; nothing is snapshotted.
  * rand    â THIS.  Not a core problem; a missing auto-seed.

FIX SHAPE (untried): seed on FIRST use, not at load â a `*p-drand48-seeded*`
flag that `%p-drand48` checks, so `srand(N); rand` stays exactly reproducible
(op/rand.t t262/t263 assert that) while an un-seeded program gets entropy.
Do NOT seed in an init hook: that would make `srand` after the hook still
reproducible but would also re-seed a saved core's state before the program
could ask for determinism, and it hides the "first use" boundary perl's own
`srand` return value documents.

NO ROW COST MEASURED â determinism is what a test suite wants, so nothing in
the gate, sweep or companion asserts the opposite.  It is a correctness bug
for real programs (a "random" temp name, a shuffle, a retry jitter).

=== DONE (s470bx, 2026-09-06) ===

FIXED in #1042's commit, in the shape this task specified and for the reason
it gave: seed on FIRST USE, not from an init hook.  perl's pp_rand seeds from
entropy when PL_srand_called is false, which is why two runs of
`perl -e 'print rand'` differ; seeding at image boot would have erased the
first-use boundary that srand's own return value documents.

  * `*p-drand48-seeded*` is the flag.  `%p-drand48` seeds through
    `%p-drand48-set-seed` when it is NIL.
  * `%p-drand48-set-seed` is now the ONE writer of `*p-drand48-state*` outside
    the draw itself â `p-srand` routes through it (rule 11), so the seeded and
    the lazy paths cannot drift.
  * `%p-drand48-entropy-seed` = (get-universal-time) XOR (pid << 13) XOR
    (get-internal-real-time).  The wall clock ALONE is not enough: two
    processes started in the same second would get the same seed and the guard
    row ("two runs differ") would flake.  It is also what an argument-less
    `srand` now returns, where it used to return (get-universal-time).
  * A boot hook clears the flag, because a saved core is the one thing that
    could arrive here already seeded (the #1042 lesson, applied to its sibling).

MEASURED vs perl 5.40.3: two runs of an unseeded program differ on both sides;
`srand(1); int rand(1000)` is 41 on both; `srand(42)` twice gives the same
three draws on both (op/rand.t t262/t263's shape).

GUARD: `Pl/t/per-run-init-01.t` rows 5-7 and 12-14 (the file is shared with
#1042 â they are one family).  Inverse-verified: the unseeded row fails on a
`git archive fcf076f1` extraction, where two runs print the same number.
subject: `p-rand` is deterministic ACROSS RUNS: `*p-drand48-state*` is seeded from a literal 0 and nothing auto-seeds it, so a program that never calls `srand` draws the SAME sequence every time.  perl auto-seeds at first use.
